title: Hackers stole ‘significant’ amount of data from tech firm relied on by thousands of US hospitals and pharmacies
teaser: A cyberattack on Craneware, a core billing software for thousands of US hospitals, stole a 'significant volume' of sensitive patient and customer data.
summary: U.K.-based Craneware, a major provider of healthcare billing software used by thousands of US hospitals and pharmacies, has suffered a cyberattack, leading to the theft of a "significant volume" of customer and employee data. While the company is working to expel the hackers, the investigation is ongoing. The incident highlights a growing and critical vulnerability in the US healthcare sector, where compromised billing software can expose vast amounts of sensitive patient medical records. This breach continues a worrying trend, following major data losses at TriZetto (3.4 million records) and the massive breach at Change Healthcare (192 million records).
author: Zack Whittaker
content: U.K.-based healthcare billing software maker Craneware is responding to a cyberattack in which hackers stole a "significant volume" of customer data from its systems, the company said on Monday. The company said the hackers appear to have been expelled from its systems, but its investigation into the breach is ongoing, according to a statement filed with the London Stock Exchange . Craneware's flagship accounting and billing software is used by thousands of clinics, hospitals, and pharmacies across the United States. The company did not say exactly what kinds of data were taken in the breach, only noting that a "percentage" of employee data, customer data, and partner records had been exfiltrated. The company, whose software helps healthcare providers bill patients for services, handles large amounts of medical records and patient data on behalf of its customers. When it bought Florida-based pharmacy software maker Sentry in 2021, Craneware said it gained access to the company's 147 million patient records that had been collected over two decades. Craneware CEO Keith Neilson did not immediately respond to TechCrunch's questions about the incident, or if the hackers have contacted the company with any demands, such as a ransom. It's not yet clear if the company's systems can receive email amid the ongoing cyberattack. While details of the hack are still under investigation, this is the latest data breach in recent months where hackers have targeted tech companies that supply tech and services to the U.S. healthcare sector. By compromising software that many healthcare providers use to analyze and understand their billing processes, hackers can access vast amounts of patient medical and health-related data, and extort the companies with threats of publicly releasing the information. Craneware is the latest health tech giant to be breached in the past year. In March, healthcare revenue tech firm TriZetto confirmed hackers stole more than 3.4 million people's personal and health data from its systems during an earlier cyberattack. That very month, medical data storage giant CareCloud reported a breach of one of its stores of patients' electronic health records , but has not yet said how much data was taken. Last July, medical billing company Episource began notifying at least 5.4 million people that their information had been stolen by hackers. The largest-ever breach of U.S. medical and healthcare data occurred in 2024, when a Russian-speaking ransomware gang hacked UnitedHealth-owned Change Healthcare. The hackers stole the medical and patient records of at least 192 million people , which the company conceded affected a "substantial proportion of people in America."

title: YouTube clarifies policies around AI slop and upsetting videos
teaser: YouTube is tightening rules against 'AI slop,' banning content that is too repetitive, emotionally distressing, or uses AI personas for sensitive topics.
summary: YouTube has updated its monetization policies to combat 'AI slop' and low-quality, inauthentic content, safeguarding the revenue generated through its Partner Program (YPP). The company clarified that three types of content cannot be monetized: 1) repetitive or template-based content; 2) 'off-putting' or distressing material; and 3) AI personas discussing sensitive subjects like finance or health. This move aims to curb 'content farming' efforts, ensuring that creators focus on high-quality, original content. With Google's video platform now earning more ad revenue than rivals, stricter policies are vital for maintaining platform quality.
author: Sarah Perez
content: A recent change sees YouTube further cracking down on AI slop by clarifying its policies around how content on its platform can be monetized. To discourage creators from using AI and other tools to make low-quality content, YouTube's policy now explains that there are three types of videos under the broader category of "inauthentic content" that cannot be monetized. YouTube already had policies around AI content. Last year, the company announced it was stemming creators' ability to generate revenue from what it called "inauthentic content," including mass-produced videos and other types of repetitive content that have become easier to generate with the help of AI technology. Rather, the recent update is about adding more nuance to the existing policies. The updated guidelines break down inauthentic content into three categories, including generic, repetitive, or template-based content, followed by off-putting or distressing content, and then any content where AI personas are used to discuss sensitive topics, like health and finance. While AI slop, much like adult content, is something of a "you'll know it when you see it" situation for many, YouTube's policies are meant to more specifically spell out when AI's use in content creation is allowed or is not permitted for videos being monetized through its YouTube Partner Program (YPP). The program, which allows creators to earn money through advertising and subscriptions, is YouTube's lifeblood; allowing it to fill up with AI slop or other low-quality fare would not be in the company's financial interests. This is especially important given that YouTube is in close competition with TV and other streamers for TV ad dollars. Google's video platform now generates more ad revenue than rival streamers and has overtaken Netflix in average daily views worldwide . As YouTube's trust and safety chief Matt Halprin explained in a Creator Insider video last week, the company's goal with its policy revision is to cut down on content farming efforts - a reference to low-quality videos that exist solely to generate revenue. "AI can actually allow people to make a lot of videos," said Halprin. "Sometimes those videos are great, and it really enhances creativity. And you can create a higher volume of high-quality content that we want to encourage and have in YPP." "But that exact same new tool can allow you to make lots of videos really quickly that are very similar. They're very generic and don't really have a narrative arc and don't really show your creativity. So the same technology really enables great stuff, but it also enables stuff that's kind of content farming, and that's the stuff that we don't want to have in YPP," Halprin added. The first category, he said, includes repetitive content, such as material that can be easily made with AI, computer-generated imagery (CGI), or templates, with little variation from video to video. This fills a channel with cookie-cutter videos. Halprin notes that tutorial videos could also fall under this policy if they're reproducing content that's already prevalent on the platform, instead of being original. The second category focuses on what YouTube calls "off-putting" content, or content designed to be distressing or emotionally manipulative to chase views. This could include videos featuring an animal in distress, which someone then comes along and rescues, Halprin said. "We've heard from our viewers that that's not something that they like. They find it off-putting. They don't want to come back to that channel, or maybe even the platform," Halprin said. Channels dedicated to this content will be removed from YPP, regardless of whether the content is AI-generated or not. The third bucket more directly targets the use of AI personas - representations of real people made with AI. YouTube says it doesn't want to incentivize creators using AI personas to discuss more sensitive topics, like finance, legal issues, healthcare, and medical issues. Any YouTube channel that has too much of any of these three types of content will not be able to monetize, Halprin said. The policy clarifications were rolled out on July 16 and impact all YouTube Partner Program members.

title: Adobe’s ‘natural look’ camera app embraces generative AI
teaser: Adobe's Project Indigo camera app is transforming with generative AI, adding tools to erase objects and turn photos into illustrations.
summary: Adobe's Project Indigo, an experimental camera app, is undergoing a major update by integrating a new 'AI Playground' suite powered by generative AI. This feature set includes Styles (applying AI-generated filters), Object Editing (which removes unwanted elements like people or clutter), Photo Guidance (providing reshoot suggestions), and Custom Edit (allowing detailed prompting). Currently utilizing Google’s Nano Banana AI, the suite is designed to enhance mobile photography by simulating complex edits previously requiring professional tools. While the app still retains manual controls like shutter speed and ISO, the AI features are tested with a limited user group. Adobe plans to gauge user adoption to determine if a paid version will be released, marking a push toward an integrated mobile camera and editing experience.
author: Jess Weatherbed
content: Adobe's experimental camera app has taken an unexpected turn. After Project Indigo was launched last year to provide a "more natural (SLR-like) look" for iPhone photography, the Indigo camera app is now being updated with a suite of generative AI tools. And the change doesn't rely upon Adobe's own Firefly AI models. Adobe describes the new "AI Playground" tooling suite as an experiment and says there's a button that allows users to opt out and continue using the app as before. Free access to the suite with no sign-on requirement is being tested with a small percentage of Indigo users over the next few weeks. "Our goal is to learn how people use GenAI-powered editing. Depending on its success we may extend the experiment, or expand the user pool, or run follow-on experiments," Adobe fellow Marc Levoy says in the announcement blog . "If the feature proves popular, we will eventually offer a paid version." The Indigo app's AI Playground, added with the version 1.1 update, includes four sections: Styles, Object Editing, Photo Guidance, and Custom Edit. Levoy says each section contains "multiple buttons or toggles, which trigger GenAI with prompts we have engineered for them." If you don't like the results of an edit, you can press the button again and " typically get something slightly different." Styles applies preset AI-generated filter effects to photographs snapped using Indigo, making them look like illustrations, changing the lighting effects, and more. Object Editing includes tools that remove people, objects, and other distractions from the backgrounds of images, with generative AI then used to fill in the blank spaces left behind, similar to Google's Magic Eraser feature. Photo Guidance is a feedback feature that allows AI to analyze your photos to provide suggestions for reshoots and editing. 1/2 Here are some before and after examples of the Indigo app's new object removal features. Image: Adobe The last feature, Custom Edit, is a broader prompting tool that lets users describe how they want to manipulate an image in more detail. For example, if you're unhappy with the results of a Styles preset, Custom Edit allows you to specify what else to change. Adobe is leaning on Google's Nano Banana AI model for this update "to start," but says it may switch or introduce additional model support over time. In this example, Adobe used the "Pen and ink" button in the Styles presets, followed by a Custom Edit to "Remove the fence in the foreground and the people in the backgroun. " Image: Adobe It's a far cry from the experience that Indigo provided at launch , with my colleague Allison describing it as a " camera app built by camera nerds for camera nerds ." It uses computational photography features to help mobile photographers capture better-quality images that re-create the look of SLR photos, alongside providing manual controls like focus, shutter speed, ISO, and white balance. The introduction of generative AI editing features may have been planned from the start, however. "This is the beginning of a journey for Adobe - towards an integrated mobile camera and editing experience that takes advantage of the latest advances in computational photography and AI," Levoy said when the Indigo app first launched . Indigo's Custom Edit tool can also be used to make paintings look like actual photographs, if that's something you want to use a photography app for... Image: Adobe Notably, the experiment also lacks the same level of consideration toward AI transparency that Adobe usually exerts . Levoy says the Indigo team is working toward adding C2PA Content Credentials - a metadata standard for identifying AI content that's already widely used by Adobe's Firefly models - to images manipulated by Indigo's generative AI tools and notes that Nano Banana already applies Google's invisible SynthID watermark . "Whether the edits you apply are 'fair' or 'misleading' depend on what you do, who you share the images with, and how you present them." Levoy says. "In the end, nothing can be implemented that reduces the importance of behaving responsibly." title: The Document Foundation says Microsoft's file formats keep users on a short leash
teaser: The Document Foundation warns that despite being an ISO standard, Microsoft's popular file formats function as a proprietary lock-in, undermining digital sovereignty.
summary: The Document Foundation (TDF) warns that ubiquitous file formats, specifically Microsoft's Office formats, create digital lock-in despite being ISO standards. While the Office Open XML (OOXML) format is standardized, TDF argues that Microsoft's implementation—favoring 'Transitional' over the cleaner 'Strict' variant—means only Microsoft's own software can correctly render the format. TDF contends that this single-implementation support makes the format functionally proprietary. The organization stresses that 'digital sovereignty' requires users to make informed choices about file format, font, and software to ensure documents display identically across systems, avoiding dependency on any single commercial vendor.
content: APPLICATIONS The Document Foundation says Microsoft's file formats keep users on a short leash OOXML may carry an ISO certificate, but only Office can be trusted to render it properly The Document Foundation (TDF) has criticized proprietary file formats and the lock-in they create, with Microsoft's ubiquitous Office formats drawing particular scrutiny. TDF would doubtless welcome a world where everyone used LibreOffice or another open equivalent, yet the reality is that Microsoft's productivity tools still dominate the office software market. However that shouldn't be a problem. Files are interchangeable these days, right? Office uses the Office Open XML (OOXML) format, so switching applications and opening .docx, .xlsx, and .pptx files should be straightforward. "The reality is considerably more complicated," TDF says . Setting aside the standardization of OOXML itself, which, TDF states, "was one of the most contested processes in the history" of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the result was OOXML Transitional, which initially coexisted with OOXML Strict. OOXML Strict, according to TDF, eliminated most of the problematic legacy elements, "but not all." Microsoft, on the other hand, defaulted to OOXML Transitional, tucking Strict at the end of the options list. "The practical effect is that the format used daily by hundreds of millions of people is the one that only Microsoft's own software implements correctly, whilst the cleaner variant - which other software could actually support - is not used, and has now even disappeared from some versions." TDF acknowledges the counterargument that the "lock-in" claims are exaggerated and that, for all the controversy surrounding its standardization, OOXML is as open a standard as any other. But TDF disagrees: "A standard that only one implementation fully supports is, from a functional point of view, a proprietary format with a standardisation certificate." The OOXML specification, which runs to thousands of pages, "did not describe a format designed for interoperability, but rather the existing behaviour of Microsoft Office, including legacy behaviours, undocumented features and implementation details specific to Microsoft's source code," TDF claims. Document lock-in has to be a factor in sovereignty considerations. "A truly independent document, one that displays identically on any system, in any country, for any user, regardless of the software used - requires informed choices at every stage of its creation." These include the format - TDF gives the example of the OpenDocument Format, used natively in LibreOffice - and even fonts to avoid a dependency on an application that might drop out of support, leaving documents effectively orphaned. Just ask anyone looking glumly at the upcoming demise of Microsoft Publisher and wondering what will become of their files. The problem with TDF's position is that it doesn't cater for the realities facing organizations with thousands, or even millions, of documents in what the group would regard as a proprietary format. PDF/A may be a viable option for archival purposes, but otherwise, the habit of relying on proprietary tools and formats is a difficult one to break. "When an institution sends a letter formatted with a proprietary font, embedded in a proprietary format, produced by proprietary software, it is not communicating information but perpetuating a dependency," TDF says. "Digital sovereignty begins with the recognition that this is a choice: the file format is a choice, the font on the page is a choice, and the software is a choice." The Register contacted Microsoft for its take on file formats that lock in users, but aside from acknowledging the question, the company has yet to respond. ®

title: LG’s glossy OLED gaming monitor is rare to find under $400
teaser: LG's 27-inch glossy WOLED gaming monitor is on sale for $379.99, offering powerful specs and a glossy finish rarely found at this price.
summary: This review compares two high-end gaming monitors: the LG 27-inch 27GX704A-B and the Asus ROG Swift 32-inch 4K QD-OLED. The LG model features a glossy WOLED panel, a 240Hz refresh rate, and is significantly discounted to $379.99, offering superior value compared to typical OLED options under $400. In contrast, the Asus monitor uses a QD-OLED panel, prized for its deep blacks, and is on sale for $899.99. Both models support fast refresh rates and variable refresh rate technology. The LG unit offers solid connectivity and an adjustable stand, while the Asus includes advanced features like a proximity sensor and a three-year burn-in warranty.
author: Sheena Vasani
content: If you've been thinking about upgrading your gaming monitor, LG's 27-inch 27GX704A-B pairs a glossy WOLED panel with a fast refresh rate, and it's currently on sale for $379.99 (about $70 off) at Amazon and directly from LG , marking a new low price. It originally launched at $799.99, but has been available for under $500 since May. The monitor offers a 1440p resolution and a glossy coating, which isn't a combination of specs we often see at this price. Most OLED monitors under $400 use QD-OLED panels, which can give blacks a slight bluish tint. LG's WOLED monitor delivers truer-looking blacks while the glossy coating helps colors appear richer and more vibrant. It doesn't sacrifice speed, either. The monitor boasts a fast 240Hz refresh rate with variable refresh rate support (Nvidia G-Sync compatible and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro), along with a fast 0.03ms response time to keep games looking sharp in motion. It comes with a solid array of ports for the price, with two HDMI 2.1 ports, DisplayPort 1.4, and USB-A ports, making it easy to connect a PC, consoles, and accessories. Rounding things out, the stand is fully adjustable, too, allowing you to raise, lower, tilt, swivel, or rotate the display into portrait mode for a more comfortable setup. Or, because it has a VESA mount, you can yank it off and toss it onto a monitor arm of your choice.

title: Hyve acquisition positions RAISE Summit for global expansion
teaser: Hyve Group acquired Chain of Events to supercharge global expansion of its tech summits, targeting massive growth in the US and EU.
summary: Hyve Group's acquisition of Chain of Events is a strategic move to turbocharge the global expansion of its major tech events, including RAISE Summit, Paris Blockchain Week, and MACHINA. The deal facilitates geographic scaling into the US and EU markets. The acquired technology is pivotal, allowing Hyve to enhance attendee deal-making and networking through curated executive roundtables, focusing on critical industry topics like AI security. title: Ford’s $30,000 electric truck: all the news about the company’s big EV re-do
teaser: Ford is scrapping its failed luxury EV approach, betting on a new $30,000 electric truck starting in 2027.
summary: After struggling with the F-150 Lightning, Ford is redesigning its EV strategy. The automaker is pivoting to a Universal Electric Vehicle Platform to create a family of low-cost EVs, starting with a new $30,000 electric truck. While the vehicle is planned for a 2027 reveal and production will start at the Kentucky assembly plant, the move comes amidst financial difficulties, marked by a staggering $19.5 billion hit on EV investments in 2025. Ford is determined to pursue EVs, focusing on efficiency and profitability rather than oversized models.
author: Andrew J. Hawkins
content: The end of the Ford F-150 Lightning was also the start of a new era for the automaker. After failing to capture the market with the electric version of its popular F-Series truck, Ford is going back to the drawing board with its Universal Electric Vehicle Platform. The first offering will be a $30,000 electric truck, engineered for efficiency and also - perhaps most importantly - profitability. The truck will be revealed in 2027, but Ford plans on building a whole family of low-cost electric vehicles at its Kentucky assembly plant. The heavily camouflaged truck has already been spotted out in the wild, with observers noting that it seems even smaller than the Maverick. Success isn't guaranteed. Ford has struggled to make profitable EVs, forcing the company to take a staggering $19.5 billion hit on its EV investments in 2025. But Ford still sees EVs as the future - just not oversize ones with "no path to profitability," as executives say.

title: X relaunches a rebuilt Android app after year-long effort
teaser: After a year, X relaunched its Android app, rebuilt from scratch to finally fix poor performance and boost global adoption.
summary: Elon Musk's X has relaunched its Android app after nearly a year, with the new version being rebuilt from scratch, rather than simply updated. According to X head of product Nikita Bier, this effort was one of the company's largest engineering projects, promising a faster, smoother, and more reliable experience. The overhaul is crucial for attracting users in global Android markets, addressing past issues like the inability to load posts when clicking links. Beyond performance boosts (loading, scrolling, notifications), the app will enable new features like video editors, Spaces support, and cashtags. Users can now update through the Google Play Store.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Nearly a year ago, Elon Musk-owned X announced it would begin rebuilding the Android version of its app, which had not held up well compared with its iOS counterpart. On Monday, the company shipped the refreshed app, which is now available to download. The new Android version of X was built from scratch and promises improvements to loading, scrolling, notifications, and more, X said in its announcement . The update has been in development for nearly a year. Last August, X head of product Nikita Bier said the social network company was putting together an Android "dream team" to reshape the experience. Later that fall, he also noted that X had one of its biggest weeks ever for Android downloads in October - a reason why the new app was a priority for the company. With today's release, Bier described the effort as "one of the largest engineering projects" in the company's history, saying the new Android app was built from scratch rather than simply being updated. "It's faster, smoother and more reliable. But most of all: it will enable us to build new features at lightning speed," Bier wrote on X. The Elon Musk-owned social network has been rolling out a number of new features in recent months, including X Money and X Chat , which were given their own standalone apps. The Android release could also potentially entice more users in global markets, where Android is the dominant smartphone platform, to either download or return to X, after years of platform neglect. ( Problems on Android were so bad at one point last year that the X app couldn't even load X posts when users clicked links.) However, Bier warned that there are still some rough edges to iron out, including improving performance on older Android devices and adding support for Spaces, X's live audio feature. Those updates are still underway. Bier added that other features, including the new video editor, the react-with-video feature, cashtags, and custom timelines are also coming soon to Android. Existing Android users can get the new X app by updating their existing app through the Google Play Store.

title: Scammers impersonate FBI on social media, prey on crime victims
teaser: ⚠️ WARNING: IC3 says any FBI account offering to recover lost funds on social media is a scam. Never trust DMs from fake agents!
summary: The FBI's IC3 issued a major warning about scammers impersonating the agency on social media to prey on cybercrime victims. These fraudsters use fake profiles, pages, and even AI-generated videos of senior FBI officials to trick people into giving up personal or financial information. IC3 warns that *no* legitimate contact regarding cybercrime recovery or complaints will happen via social media, phone, or email. The center stresses that its IC3 does not have a social media presence. To avoid falling victim, the public should treat any direct contact from these fake accounts as fraudulent, regardless of how convincing the scam appears.
content: security Scammers impersonate FBI on social media, prey on crime victims IC3 says any account claiming to represent it is fake Real FBI agents won't slide into your DMs and offer to help you recover stolen funds. The bureau's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) update d an earlier warning on Monday about scammers impersonating the agency online, saying fraudsters continue to use the scheme "to deceive and revictimize individuals." According to IC3, there are two different schemes being used to target cybercrime victims, both directly and by soliciting them to report incidents. In the first scheme, IC3 said scammers create fraudulent social media profiles and pages impersonating FBI personnel or IC3. They may also infiltrate online groups for fraud victims or contact victims directly while claiming to represent the FBI or the complaint center. In other cases, victims are being contacted by someone claiming to be an FBI agent after realizing they were approached by someone trying to scam them and saying they intended to report the incident to the FBI or file an IC3 complaint. The FBI said the impersonator then directs victims to a fake IC3 update page or continues communicating through messaging apps. In the other instance, scammers are creating AI-generated videos on social media depicting senior FBI officials and directing users to a spoofed IC3 website to report cybercrimes they may have fallen victim to, with the scammers then collecting the information and using it to contact victims for further fraud. AI-generated depictions of public figures are similarly being used to make such scams appear legitimate. "Some individuals received an email or a phone call, while others were approached, or observed an advertisement via social media or forums," the IC3 said. "Almost all complainants indicated the scammers claimed to have recovered the victim's lost funds or offered to assist in recovering funds." Regardless of how legitimate social media profiles look, or how realistic those AI-generated videos may be, the IC3 is warning that none of them should be believed for a simple reason: The IC3 doesn't have a social media presence of any kind, and it doesn't investigate crimes or offer to recover lost funds through social media. "Any social media profiles or pages claiming to represent IC3 or offering to recover lost money are fraudulent and are actively attempting to steal your personal or financial information," the IC3 warned. "IC3 will never directly communicate with individuals via phone, email, social media, phone apps, online chat, or public forums." The IC3 said that any contact made with a cybercrime victim who reports an incident via its actual website will be made by an FBI employee from a local field office or other law enforcement official. Here's another hot tip: If you fall victim to a cybercrime or online scam, don't post about it on social media - that's only going to invite someone with bad intentions to seek you out. ®

title: The Odyssey turned me into an IMAX believer
teaser: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey requires the immersive scale of 70mm IMAX film to fully capture its epic scope, revealing visual details missed in standard screenings.
summary: The viewing experience of Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s epic, *The Odyssey*, drastically changes based on the format. While beautiful in any theater, the full scale of the story requires 70mm film IMAX. In the 70mm format (1.43:1), massive creatures like the Cyclops Polyphemus and the sea monster Scylla appear far more gigantic, offering greater detail than the 35mm format (2.39:1). This immersive size makes the film's visual elements more impactful. However, the format's scarcity is a challenge: only about 40 theaters globally can screen the 70mm film, and IMAX faces hurdles in securing theater investment for necessary screen retrofits.
author: Charles Pulliam-Moore
content: After seeing Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey for the first time early last week, I came away impressed, but somewhat conflicted about two of the film's more fantastical set pieces. While those scenes were beautifully crafted and tremendously acted, there was something a little bit off about the way they hit my eye. I spent days wondering what, exactly, wasn't quite working for me during that first theatrical viewing, and I thought that might have just been splitting hairs. But it wasn't until I saw the movie again over the weekend - this time in IMAX - that the issue became crystal clear. Though I'd heard all of the buzz about The Odyssey being the first feature shot entirely with 70mm film IMAX cameras , I thought a lot of it was clever marketing hype meant to activate Nolan's cinephile fan base. I hadn't considered how watching the film in larger format would make for a markedly different viewing experience. But The Odyssey really is a movie that needs to be seen in IMAX if you want to get a true sense of the story Nolan is telling. Spoiler warning: This story contains spoilers for The Odyssey (which, to be fair, is an adaptation of Homer's almost 3,000-year-old epic poem). There are many scenes throughout The Odyssey that look perfectly fine when the film is displayed in the 35mm format. Majestic, wide shots of Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his men at sea make you appreciate the Mediterranean's expansiveness, and you can feel the soldiers' claustrophobic tension as they hide within the Trojan horse. Even though you can see that the film is cropped, Odysseus' disastrous encounter with the Laestrygonians gives you a sense of how gigantic they are compared to the wandering Ithacans. But The Odyssey 's scenes involving some of the story's more gargantuan monsters take on a different gravity when they're displayed in IMAX because of how much more visual information there is to take in. When I saw The Odyssey in 35mm - which is projected in a widescreen, 2.39:1 aspect ratio - I knew that the Cyclops Polyphemus (Bill Irwin) towered over the humans who marched into his cave searching for food. But when I saw a standard IMAX screening of the film - whose 1.90:1 aspect ratio is smaller than the 70mm's 1.43:1 ratio - I had a much clearer understanding of the creature's stature and the subtle nuances baked into Irwin's physical performance. Because the IMAX screening projected a taller image, I was able to spend more time taking in details that were easy to miss the first time around, like the way Polyphemus has to hunch in order to keep his head from hitting the cave's ceiling. The substantive difference between the two screenings became exceedingly obvious once I saw the Cyclops chasing Odysseus and his men down a mountain for a second time. In 70mm, you can see more of the monster's upper body as it lumbers through trees in a fitful rage, which brings an added sense of danger and urgency to the chase scene. I had a similar experience seeing the soldiers rowing past a whirlpool not knowing that they were drifting directly into the sea monster Scylla's reach. The 35mm screening shows you that Scylla's humongous, but the IMAX screening's added real estate makes it easier to understand how she's able to snatch her victims up before any of them realize that she's lurking in the cliffs above them. By shooting The Odyssey completely in 70mm, Nolan crafted a film whose size and visual detail could make it feel immersive in ways that most modern features aren't. But he also chose a format that makes it difficult for most theatergoers to see the movie in its most impressive form. Because there are only about 40 theaters globally (25 in the US) that are able to screen 70mm IMAX films, the vast majority of people will probably never get a chance to take The Odyssey in as Nolan intended. This and the fact that standard IMAX screenings are more expensive than standard movies have prompted some to accuse the director of being anti-art and contributing to the culture of obsessive format purism . One could also argue that Nolan is using The Odyssey to show IMAX and theater owners that there is a genuine public demand for films shot in 70mm. The current shortage of 70mm screenings of The Odyssey is due to the fact that IMAX hasn't been able to produce new projectors. Speaking to Variety , IMAX CEO Richard Gelfond explained that the company has largely been focused on retrofitting old projectors, but there aren't many movie exhibitors willing to take on the construction costs it would take to build the 1.43:1 screens necessary to display 70mm films. If IMAX and various theater chains were willing to pony up the cash for projector part development and venue expansion, 70mm screenings could become more common. But for the time being, the industry seems comfortable using the format's scarcity as an effective marketing tool. That marketing strategy has worked for The Odyssey - a highly anticipated project from one of the world's most revered filmmakers. But Nolan's star power clearly has a lot to do with the movie's box office success . There aren't that many other directors who could get people journeying across the country just to see one of their features. It also helps that the movie is actually worth seeing, especially in IMAX.

title: The FCC is planning to retroactively ban disguised DJI gadgets
teaser: The FCC plans to retroactively ban 'DJI front companies,' threatening to remove pre-approved gadgets like the Osmo Pocket 3 from US shelves.
summary: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is preparing to exercise its retroactive authority by targeting several 'front companies' suspected of circumventing US foreign drone bans using Chinese technology, particularly relating to DJI. The FCC has proposed a $25,000 fine on eight such companies and, critically, plans to ban them from importing, distributing, or selling existing drones and cameras. This ban could force products, like Xtra's version of the Osmo Pocket 3, off major retailers' sites. The FCC claims national security concerns but the ban would not affect items already purchased. Targeted firms include Cogito Tech, Xtra Technology, and others, with the actions initially flagged by Konrad Iturbe. The FCC is also terminating its relationship with the Chinese test lab SGS-CSTC Shenzhen.
author: Sean Hollister
content: Last October, we told you how the FCC had given itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets that have already received its approval to be imported and sold in the United States. Now, the FCC's getting ready to wield that power for the first time, by cracking down on the "DJI front companies" suspected of sneaking the Chinese company's tech past its foreign drone ban . Two Fridays ago, the FCC had already proposed a $25,000 fine on eight of those "front companies," including the ones behind the Skyrover drones and Xtra cameras . But now, the FCC is proposing a lot more than a slap-on-the-wrist - it's planning to ban those same companies from continuing to import, distribute, market, and sell their existing drones and cameras. For example, we highlighted a deal on Xtra's version of the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 just two weeks ago, a product that already got FCC approval before the drone ban ever came down, and a proudct which Amazon offers with next-day shipping. If the FCC's retroactive ban goes into effect, that product should disappear from all major online retailers and Xtra's own website, and the company may even need to write off however many cameras are still sitting in US warehouses like Amazon's. The ban wouldn't affect gadgets that have already been purchased, and it wouldn't happen immediately. The FCC's currently taking public comments for 30 days first. While the FCC has "tentatively" concluded that these companies are selling equipment that should be banned over national security fears, it claims it'll listen to "specific evidence" otherwise. But that should maybe be taken with a grain of salt: the FCC largely ignored public comments about net neutrality and lied about a cyberattack . It's also worth pointing out that the US government has never provided specific public evidence that foreign drones pose a national security threat to begin with, or why other products like cameras should be caught up in that ban. If you want to comment anyhow, you can do so with an "Express Filing" here . In the meantime, the FCC says it has "temporarily deferred the grantee codes of these companies," a phrase that it does not define. (A former FCC official tells The Verge he's never heard that phrase before; we're asking the FCC if that means these companies can't get future gadgets authorized for import and sale.) The specific companies that the FCC is targeting include Cogito Tech, Fixaxo Technology, Lyno Dynamics, Skyhigh Tech, Spatial Hover, SZ Knowact and WaveGo Tech (both of whom are behind Skyrover), and Xtra Technology, none of which responded to the FCC's requests for information. It also includes agricultural drone brand XAG, which did reportedly reply to the FCC once, but not with the information that the FCC asked for. All save XAG were brought to the FCC's attention by Konrad Iturbe, who figured out how to track the "FCC front companies" last year. The FCC also cites our story about Xtra . Today, the FCC is also announcing that it's parting ways with one of the Chinese test labs that helped some of these products make it to market: SGS-CSTC Shenzhen. While SGS-CSTC did reply to the FCC to claim it's not controlled by the Chinese government, as the China-owned CSTC only has 15 percent ownership of the lab, US law currently considers another entity to have control if it has 10 percent or more or a company - at least when it comes to authorizing radios for use in the US. On July 10th, the FCC said it might take even more actions against the eight "DJI front companies" if they didn't reply by today, July 20th. We'll let you know what we hear.

title: Technology — AI divides grow at top firms
teaser: Despite fears of job apocalypse, AI reports suggest radiology staff is growing, with AI tools improving workflows by over 26% without replacing workers.
summary: A new report by Build American AI counters widespread fears that artificial intelligence will eliminate professional jobs, citing the radiology field as evidence. The group notes that jobs in radiology have increased, despite earlier predictions of decline. Data shows the Mayo Clinic's radiology staff rose by 55% (2016-2025), and HPI reported a 17.3% increase in Medicare-affiliated radiologist numbers. While AI is used to improve workflows—such as cutting documentation time by 15.5% and decreasing patient stay by 26.3% at Northwestern Medicine—it is portrayed as a tool, not a substitute for American workers. The group directly challenges the 2016 warnings of 'godfather of AI,' Geoffrey Hinton, who cautioned about the field's future.
author: The Hill
content: The AI advocacy group Build American AI released a new report Monday highlighting how AI did not kill the field of radiology as some predicted ten years ago, with jobs in the field actually increasing over the past decade. The group is honing in on the radiology example as polling shows more than half of Americans are about losing their jobs due to AI. first shared with The Hill, cites a number of external statistics from the Mayo Clinic and Harvey L. Nieman Health Policy Institute showing a growth in radiology staff in the U.S. Mayo Clinic reported increased by 55 percent between 2016 and 2025 The clinic touts nearly 400 radiologists today. Meanwhile, HPI found the number of radiologists working in U.S. Medicare-affiliated practices increased from 30,723 to 36,024, a 17.3 percent increase , per the report. This does not mean AI is not being used in the radiology department, but is changing the workflow for radiologists, the group says. At Northwestern Medicine, generative AI tools cut radiology documentation time by 15.5 percent, while "AI-assisted workflows" decreased patients' length stay for pulmonary embolism cases by 26.3 percent. Build American AI, the advocacy arm of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, argues these statistics go against the warnings from Geoffrey Hinton, the so-called "godfather of AI," who said in 2016 people should "stop training radiologists now." Hinton's claim, Build American AI argues, led to increased fears around job loss in the AI sector. AI industry leaders themselves have the technology could disrupt the labor market, with predictions ranging from a so-called job apocalypse to scenarios where AI changes the nature of work without triggering mass layoffs. But Nathan Leamer , the group's executive director, says the radiology industry will "follow throughout the American economy." "AI is not a substitute for American workers, it is a tool for American workers," Leamer said.

title: AI materials science startup CuspAI raises $450M in funding
teaser: AI startup CuspAI raises $450M, using its MIRA platform to cut years of material science research into mere months.
summary: CuspAI Ltd., a U.K.-based AI materials science startup, announced a $450 million funding round, valuing the company at $2.6 billion. CuspAI's mission is to accelerate the discovery of materials essential for future industrial progress. They developed MIRA, an AI platform that significantly speeds up the typically years-long process of identifying and simulating new compounds. MIRA utilizes two open-source tools: UMA, which simulates compounds at the atomic level, and kUPS, which simulates molecular structure. To maximize its impact, CuspAI also formed the AI Materials Foundry, a consortium including tech giants like Nvidia, Samsung, and Meta. The foundry aims to leverage MIRA to rapidly identify material candidates for industrial applications, such as advanced chip interconnects.
author: Maria Deutscher
content: CuspAI Ltd., a startup using artificial intelligence to discover new materials, today announced that it has raised $450 million in funding. The U.K.-based company also formed a chemical research consortium that includes Nvidia Corp. and Samsung Electronics Co. CuspAI's Series B round values it at $2.6 billion. The deal was led by Kleiner Perkins and NEA with a "significant contribution" from Bezos Expeditions. The funds were joined by more than a half-dozen others, including prominent tech investor John Doerr. Discovering a new compound requires scientists to navigate trillions of material and molecular structure combinations. In the initial phase of a chemistry project, research teams narrow down the possibilities to a relatively small number of promising compound candidates. They then test the candidates in a simulation to evaluate their properties. CuspAI has developed an AI platform called MIRA that speeds up the process. According to the company, the software can complete tasks that usually take years in six months. It does so using two open-source projects called UMA and kUPS. UMA is a series of AI models that Meta Platforms Inc. released last year. The algorithms can simulate compounds at the atomic level to map out their electronic properties. Those electronic properties, in turn, can help researchers understand important details such as how a newly discovered compound interacts with other materials. The other open-source technology that underpins MIRA, kUPS, was developed by CuspAI. Whereas UMA simulates materials at the atomic level, kUPS does so at the molecular level. The latter approach lends itself better to tasks such as understanding the internal structure of crystals. In addition to analyzing molecules, kUPS can automate certain coding tasks. Graphics cards sometimes struggle to process datasets that contain information collected at both the atomic and molecular levels. Developers can use kUPS to increase the efficiency with which such data is processed. Additionally, the toolkit makes it easier to troubleshoot simulation errors. CuspAI developed MIRA using several academic datasets to which it bought exclusive AI training rights. The company also used information from popular scientific journals. MIRA underpins the AI Materials Foundry, a new research consortium that CuspAI launched in conjunction with its funding announcement. The group comprises more than 45 members, including Nvidia, Samsung, Meta and other tech industry heavyweights. Its goal is to speed up material discovery. AI Materials Foundry members can ask MIRA to discover new compounds. For example, a chipmaker could request a material that lends itself to building interconnects. MIRA identifies material candidates and sends them to a lab that can manufacture them. It picks the most suitable facility based on factors such as its production capacity. "If we don't make progress fast, the next 50 years of industrial progress will be constrained by a single challenge: the world needs materials that don't yet exist," said CuspAI Chief Executive Officer Chad Edwards (pictured, right, with co-founder Max Welling). "That's what we're on a mission to solve - combining frontier agentic AI with deep domain expertise, exclusive data access and close customer partnerships." CuspAI will use its newly raised funding to grow its international presence. title: Colossal Biosciences reportedly in talks to raise new capital at $20B–$30B valuation
teaser: Colossal Biosciences, the de-extinction startup, is raising capital at an astronomical $20B–$30B valuation.
summary: De-extinction startup Colossal Biosciences is reportedly targeting a massive $20B–$30B valuation in its next round of funding. Co-founded by Ben Lamm, the company generates revenue through diverse applications, including government contracts with the U.S. and UAE ($60 million invested). Its scientific work has spawned profitable ventures like Form Bio and Astromech ($2B valuation). Beyond resurrecting species like the woolly mammoth, Colossal is developing technologies such as artificial animal wombs for potential human fertility treatments and adding new targets like the bluebuck antelope. Success in de-extinction could also lead to revenue from biodiversity credits.
author: Marina Temkin
content: When de-extinction startup Colossal Biosciences revealed last year that it was attempting to "resurrect" the dire wolf from genetic material found in fossils , we argued that, despite the controversy surrounding the project, the company was building valuable technologies that justify its $10.2 billion valuation. Now, roughly 16 months later, the startup is in talks to raise new funding at a $20 billion to $30 billion valuation, Axios reported . It's not clear who is leading the new round, or how much capital the five-year-old company is looking to raise. But we do know, according to the report, that Colossal has started generating revenue over the last year. Colossal co-founder and CEO Ben Lamm told TechCrunch last year that the company sees three revenue streams for the business. The company has offered its conservation technology to the U.S. government and the UAE, which recently invested $60 million in the company, according to Wired. Colossal has spun out three startups, including Breaking, a company that helps break down plastics; Form Bio, a computational biology platform that secured $30 million in funding; and Astromech, an AI-driven predictive modeling company focused on biology and life sciences, which was valued at $2 billion in March. The company, which operates out a 55,000-square-foot headquarters in Dallas , keeps finding new applications for its core science, too. In late April, it added the bluebuck antelope as its sixth target species, while late last month, its nonprofit conservation arm, the Colossal Foundation, struck a University of Tasmania partnership to help protect Tasmanian devils from a contagious facial cancer . Lamm told TechCrunch last year that the company also plans to spin off its artificial animal womb technology, which could have applications for human fertility treatment. In May, he told Rolling Stone that the technology is expected to be ready next year. If the company manages to reintroduce extinct animals, including the woolly mammoth and the dodo bird, to their native habitats, it may eventually generate revenue through the sale of biodiversity credits, a market-based mechanism similar to carbon credits, according to Lamm. The new fundraising effort comes amid a boom in longevity tech, alternative energy, and other deep-tech sectors. Colossal didn't respond to our request for comment.

title: Microsoft Open-Sources Comic Chat, but It Is No Relaunch
teaser: A 1996 chat app turned text into comic strips using fixed rules, predating modern AI generations.
summary: Microsoft has open-sourced the code for Comic Chat, a pioneering 1996 visual IRC client. Originally developed by David Kurlander in 1995, the system transformed standard text-based chat into illustrated comic panels, complete with characters and expressive artwork. Critically, Comic Chat was not an image generator; instead, it used human-written rules to map conversational cues (like expressing anger) to fixed, predefined comic assets supplied by artist Jim Woodring. Microsoft released the code in July 2024 as a historical, MIT-licensed archive. While the archive includes experimental modernizations for current tools, it is explicitly noted that it is not a continuously maintained product, offering developers a valuable look at early 2000s visual communication systems.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Open-Source Archive: Microsoft has published Comic Chat's code under the MIT License as a historical archive for reuse, modification, and redistribution. Archive Contents: The repository combines four historical snapshots with experimental modernization examples designed for current development tools. Modernization Limits: The experimental examples cover high-resolution display scaling, modern Internet Relay Chat connections, and optional encryption without promising production readiness. Rules-Based Design: Comic Chat used human-written rules and artist-drawn assets to turn text-chat cues into comic panels. Microsoft made Comic Chat's source code public on July 16 alongside experimental modernization examples. Originally introduced in 1996, the visual Internet Relay Chat (IRC) client turned typed conversations into illustrated panels with characters, speech bubbles, expressions, and gestures. For preservation and experimentation, the MIT-licensed historical archive uses a permissive open-source license that allows modification and redistribution. Microsoft characterizes the updated builds as worked examples rather than polished re-releases, and the archive is not actively maintained. Comic Chat used human-written rules to map words and other textual cues to predefined artwork. Unlike image-generating systems that create new images from learned examples, it selected fixed drawings and arranged them into a conversation. How Comic Chat Turns Text Into Panels Comic Chat creator David Kurlander began the project inside Microsoft Research in 1995. Kurlander and his team tested the idea by asking comic artist Jim Woodring to illustrate real text-chat transcripts . Woodring supplied the characters and visual treatment. Microsoft's team translated choices such as poses, expressions, balloon shapes, layouts, and zoom levels into software rules. Software rules tied every automated visual choice to artwork and behavior that the team had defined in advance. Comic Chat uses an expert system to determine character placement , gestures, facial expressions, balloon shape, and panel layout in real time. A cue can change a character's expression or gesture, speech balloon, camera distance, or panel arrangement. Developers can follow a message through a defined rule to the chosen drawing, making each visual decision inspectable instead of hiding it inside a generated result. Comic Chat also extended IRC messages with metadata for character state, poses, and panel information. Some networks auto-kicked its users when standard clients encountered the additional traffic. Microsoft operated dedicated Comic Chat servers alongside that extended behavior. Comic Chat remained interoperable with IRC after MSN shut those servers in 2001. Its visual layer depended on both local rules and cooperation from the surrounding network. Prepared assets imposed a clear creative limit. While Comic Chat can recombine existing characters and expressions, it cannot not create an unseen pose or improvise another visual style. Interface researchers can compare the trigger, rule, and resulting panel to study how Woodring's artistic choices became repeatable software behavior inside a live communication tool. Microsoft's repository preserves both the client code and a legible example of 1990s human-computer interaction design. Microsoft built the original client with Visual C++ 4.0 and Microsoft Foundation Classes before distributing it with Internet Explorer 3 in 1996. It later bundled Comic Chat with Windows 98 and Internet Explorer 4 and 5 and made it MSN's official chat client. Comic Chat was localized into 24 languages , while Kurlander's firsthand project history puts its reach at millions of users worldwide. Its broad distribution gives the code value beyond nostalgia. Developers can examine a visual communication system that operated at consumer scale rather than surviving only as a research prototype. What the Open Code Does Not Promise Four historical snapshots cover a 1996 prerelease, version 1.0 from 1996, a February 1998 version 2.1 beta, and a June 1998 version 2.5 beta. Modernization folders build with Microsoft's Visual Studio software-development environment and add scaling for high-resolution displays plus modern IRC server and optional TLS support . Transport Layer Security (TLS) encrypts a network connection; it does not establish that the old network code is secure or production-ready. Microsoft's modernization folders are experimental examples layered onto those historical snapshots, not a continuously maintained successor branch. They demonstrate how parts of the client can compile with current tools and connect under newer network conditions. Four snapshots also preserve differences between prerelease and beta-era code. Developers have concrete migration examples without a promise that every archived version follows the same path or receives future fixes. High-resolution scaling and server changes remove specific barriers for Windows developers, but they do not test long-term stability across IRC networks. Contributors will also have to manage future server changes and distribute updates to users. Existing IRC clients illustrate the maintenance work a supported application requires. HexChat ended official releases in 2024 , although its code, documentation, installers, and dependencies remain available for forks. WeeChat remains an active multi-platform IRC-focused client with encrypted connections, authentication, scripting, and remote interfaces. Neither condition makes Comic Chat a current competitor. Its repository offers material for preservation and experimentation, not an application with an operating support channel. Contributors will have to publish and maintain a fork that connects reliably to modern IRC servers before Windows users have a supported Comic Chat application.

title: Avengers: Doomsday’s first trailer puts everyone on high alert
teaser: The new 'Avengers: Doomsday' trailer reveals a massive clash of heroes, centering on Robert Downey Jr.'s chaotic Doctor Doom.
summary: The first trailer for 'Avengers: Doomsday' has been released, promising a massive spectacle involving multiple hero factions. While Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom appears central to the chaos, the movie seems to feature multiple hero teams—including the X-Men, Fantastic Four, and New Avengers—who must unite against a common enemy. Thor and Steve Rogers are positioned to bring these disparate groups together. The film is scheduled for release on December 18th, with additional details expected at San Diego Comic-Con.
author: Charles Pulliam-Moore
content: After months of teasing us with reminders about how large Avengers: Doomsday 's cast is going to be , Marvel has finally released a proper trailer for the film. Though Robert. Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom definitely appears to be causing a lot of the chaos in Doomsday 's first trailer, the movie seems like it's going to feature more than a few moments where different teams of heroes fight one another. Thor (Chris Hemsworth) seems to be the only person who understands that the X-Men , the Fantastic Fou r, and the (New) Avengers need to be more focused on dealing with their new Latverian enemy . And while Thor might not be able to rally the troops on his own, Steve Rogers' (Chris Evans) presence will probably bring them all together. The trailer makes Doomsday seem like it's going to be another humongous spectacle that puts a lot of emphasis on our nostalgia for Marvel's old X-Men movies. Marvel probably has a few more Doomsday details we won't hear about until the studio comes to San Diego Comic-Con later this week, which should get people even more hyped to see the film before it hits theaters on December 18th - the same day that Dune: Part Three hits theaters.

title: The AirPods Max 2 are down to their second-best price
teaser: AirPods Max 2 are on sale for $449 during 'Black Friday in July,' featuring advanced H2 wireless chip capabilities like live translation.
summary: The AirPods Max 2 are currently discounted to $449 at both Amazon and Best Buy, representing $100 off the typical price. Although this is higher than the previous Prime Day price of $399.99, the deal is available during the 'Black Friday in July' sale. The Max 2 boasts significant internal improvements, including USB-C connectivity and a powerful built-in amp. Furthermore, the inclusion of the H2 wireless chip provides advanced functionalities such as live translation, adaptive audio, and conversation awareness, making it attractive for users upgrading from the original model.
author: Cameron Faulkner
content: There are a ton of deals available to shop today thanks to Best Buy's "Black Friday in July" sale lasting all week. The sale typically aligns closely with Prime Day each year, but of course, Amazon's shopping holiday happened much earlier than we expected. So it's nice to have some deals in July. One of example of a great deal is Apple's AirPods Max 2 , which are down to $449 at Amazon and Best Buy , $100 off their usual price. It's only the second time they've been discounted. Prime Day knocked them all the way down to $399.99, but today's price isn't bad at all if you missed out last month. They're available at this price in every color. Our review called the Max 2 a "great sequel, but not an ambitious one." In short, not much has changed, especially in terms of design. There are some internal improvements that might make it worth it for those who have the original iteration (especially if you have the model with the Lightning connector). The Max 2 features USB-C connectivity like the 2024 revision, but has a built-in amp that delivers incredible sound that edges out the competition, not to mention the H2 wireless chip that enables features like live translation, adaptive audio, and conversation awareness.

title: LG’s monitors come with an unwanted addition for Windows: McAfee pop-up ads
teaser: New LG monitors silently force auto-installation of apps and pop up McAfee ads on Windows 11, bypassing user consent.
summary: New LG monitors pose a privacy concern for Windows 11 users due to the silent auto-installation of associated software. Upon connection, the LG Monitor App Installer, often via Windows Update, installs without user permission, leading to intrusive pop-up ads for McAfee and various LG apps. Although Microsoft allows developers to automatically pair hardware support apps, the LG program requires permissions to use 'all system resources' and collect device/internet data. Frustrated users must employ workarounds: Windows Pro users can apply group policy settings, and Home edition users can adjust advanced system settings to prevent the unwanted setup.
author: Stevie Bonifield
content: A video from Gamers Nexus explains how, after connecting a new LG UltraGear monitor to a PC running Windows 11 for the first time, Windows Update is silently installing LG driver updates and the LG Monitor App Installer, without so much as a permission pop-up or notification. The app doesn't appear to include special controls of its own, instead simply pointing users to LG's other apps, as well as McAfee antivirus. There are reports about LG's app auto-installing as far back as 2024 , but Gamers Nexus's test follows recent user complaints on Reddit about large pop-up ads for McAfee and LG's own apps suddenly appearing in the bottom right corner of the homescreen, which popped up for GN on 31 out of 32 bootups. Microsoft allows developers to pair a Hardware Support App in the Windows Store that automatically installs based on the device's metadata, but even its description here includes a warning: The automatic installation feature does not provide a notification to the user when the app is installed. Some users may find this experience confusing and frustrating, and give your app a bad rating. As The Verge 's Tom Warren has pointed out in the past , Dell similarly auto-installs its Alienware Command Center app on Windows when you connect an Alienware monitor, but the notification spam is an extra twist. Users have reported ways to block LG's app from auto-installing by applying a group policy setting on Pro versions of Windows, while users of Home editions might be able to turn off the installation by selecting "No" on an option to automatically download manufacturers' apps and custom icons that is inside the Advanced system settings section. As Gamers Nexus mentions, according to its Windows Store page , the LG Monitor App Installer requires permission to "use all system resources" and "access your Internet connection," and the linked LG privacy policy mentions automatically collecting device data, internet activity, and geolocation information - all for a program that's installing without the user's explicit permission or consent.

title: The PlayStation replica ornament is an homage to a great, yet fragile console
teaser: The iconic PlayStation chime is actually a multi-part sound requiring disc recognition. See the detailed new ornament replica!
summary: A new Hallmark Keepsake ornament replicates the PlayStation console (pre-DualShock version), offering a nostalgic tribute to a classic gaming system. The replica is highly detailed, featuring elements like the ridged sides, power plug, and A/V port, with the controller glued to the disc lid. Upon activation, a green LED lights up and plays the console's signature multi-part boot chime, which historically required the machine to recognize a disc. The ornament is available for $28.99, serving as an elegant and fun memento for fans.
author: Cameron Faulkner
content: You probably know the signature PlayStation boot sound . Did you know that it's technically a multi-part chime? There's the synthy section where "Sony Computer Entertainment" shows onscreen with a white background. You only get to the next screen with the echo-y chimes and the color-filled PlayStation logo if your console recognizes the disc. How badly I wanted my sorta-broken console to get to that second screen. My console's disc spindle came apart pretty early into me owning it. As an eight-year-old kid, fixing the spindle was the riskiest undertaking of my life yet. The internet wasn't really a haven for how-tos yet, so I superglued that thing, and it worked, sort of. But the spindle is supposed to be flexible to let the disc on and off (it had a rubber ring with small ball bearings in there, too - the mechanisms were blowing my mind at the time). So, pieces came off regularly, and I would just glue them back on and keep gaming. The wait for the second part of the boot chime to activate on my console was agonizing. It would sometimes take close to 10 seconds, or not happen at all. The upside is that it my gaming time more precious, and it made Hallmark's new Keepsake ornament of the console hit harder than I expected it to. The company's running series of console replicas is great, and its previous one was the Xbox 360 replica last year. It's cool to see one made for a console with an even bigger legacy (one that's not tainted by a widespread hardware issue). The PlayStation changed my relationship with gaming, as well as my relationship with tech. The ornament celebrates the pre-DualShock version of the console. There are a lot of lovely details, like the ridged sides, the power plug, and the A/V port that Sony stuck with through the PlayStation 3. The controller is glued to the disc lid of the console, and its flexible cable is partially glued to its side. Upon pressing the power button, a green LED lights up, and the PlayStation chime plays in full - both parts. There are a few little imperfections that I noticed on my unit out of the box, and the power button's font is a little crooked, but nothing that's easy to notice at a couple feet away. $28.99 for the ornament will either seem a bit steep, or totally acceptable, depending on how nostalgia-addled you are for this era of gaming. I've always been the kind of gamer who likes what I like without having to be loud about it. The ornament, like Hallmark's other Keepsake models, is elegant and not too flashy. It's just a PlayStation that can chill in a tree come time for the holidays. It's also a fun memento that represents a great console that I played to pieces that I can display whenever and wherever I want.

content: The aptly-named "2K Megahits 2026 Bundle" from Humble includes 15 Steam games for $15. title: Copper Holds Firm as China Stocks Shrink
teaser: Copper prices remain steady despite global pressure, driven by shrinking copper inventories in China, signaling tight physical supply.
summary: Copper prices are holding firm despite macroeconomic pressures, largely due to a key physical market signal: diminishing supply in China. According to analysis citing Goldman Sachs, visible copper cathode stocks in China have fallen to the bottom end of their historical seasonal range, suggesting limited refined copper supplies in the world's largest consumer market. Industry leaders, such as Robert Friedland, point to this decline, alongside rising cancelled warrants in London Metal Exchange warehouses, as evidence of tightening physical availability. The article also mentions Canadian Copper's (CSE: CCI) focus on developing VMS deposits in New Brunswick, Canada.
author: The Deep Dive
content: Sponsored by Canadian Copper Copper Holds Firm as China Stocks Shrink Copper prices are holding firm despite a series of macroeconomic pressures that would normally weigh on industrial metals, with traders increasingly focused on a physical market signal: China's shrinking copper inventories. Visible copper cathode stocks in China have fallen to the bottom end of their historical seasonal range, according to data presented in a Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research exhibit using Wind and Shanghai Metals Market data. The decline suggests that available refined copper supplies in the world's largest copper-consuming market are becoming increasingly limited relative to recent years. Robert Friedland, founder and executive chairman of Ivanhoe Mines, highlighted the Goldman Sachs research in a social media post, pointing to falling Chinese inventories and rising cancelled warrants in London Metal Exchange warehouses as signs of tightening physical availability. You can read more on the matter here . Canadian Copper (CSE: CCI) is focused on the exploration and development of the largest VMS deposits across its ~8,600 hectares in the well-known Bathurst Mining Camp in New Brunswick Canada. Canadian Copper is currently in the process of consolidating the Caribou Plant Complex, with a permitted 3,000 tpd mine and mill, with their flagship Murray Brook asset that boasts a resource of 21 million tonnes at 1.42% copper equivalent measured and indicated. title: Comment in code read 'Dear future me, sorry I wrote this'
teaser: Years after fixing an intermittent bug, a programmer found a code comment he wrote himself: 'Dear future Johnny, I am very, very sorry.'
summary: In an anecdote shared in the 'Who, Me?' column, programmer Johnny details a struggle with an elusive, intermittent software bug. Initially hired for Visual Basic, he developed the failing system using C#. The complex string manipulation routine would glitch, working perfectly about half the time before failing completely. The bug mysteriously resolved itself after random code adjustments. Years later, while investigating the persistent error, Johnny found a chilling code comment written by himself: "Dear future Johnny, I am very, very sorry." The story highlights the unpredictability of software bugs and the lingering impact of developer work.
content: software Comment in code read 'Dear future me, sorry I wrote this' Developer was hired to write VB, used C# instead, and thought he mostly made it work WHO, ME? Regrets? We've had a few. And so have many readers of The Register, who we try to help by getting their stories of workplace mistakes off their chests every Friday in a reader-contributed column we call "Who, Me?" This week, meet a reader who asked to be Regomized as "Johnny," who told us he was once hired as a Visual Basic developer, a job he thought was beneath him. He got on with things anyway, until he was given a new project that he decided to write in C# despite that language being new at the time. "To my satisfaction, it handled everything the customer required," Johnny told The Register . But then he hit trouble. A complex string manipulation routine that determined how tasks were routed started to glitch. "About half the time, it worked perfectly. The rest of the time, it failed completely," Johnny wrote. "I stepped through the code repeatedly, checking every transformation, every condition, every variable - but nothing stood out as wrong." He therefore started making small and random changes in the hope it would flush the bug into the open. One of those changes broke everything, so Johnny reverted it - and after that the glitch magically disappeared. "I compared versions, searched for differences, retraced my steps - and found no reason," he told The Register . "To this day, I have no idea what caused it or why it disappeared." Over time, the incident faded from Johnny's memory. Several years later, Johnny was still at the company and had climbed the career ladder to become a senior developer. "One day, the support team escalated an issue to me: an intermittent bug that no one could solve. I agreed to take a look," he said. His first step was to look for comments in the code to understand the intent of whoever wrote this piece of software. "Scrolling through the header, I found the author's note originally written by myself and felt an immediate sense of dread," he told Who, Me? That sense was prescient because the comment read: "Dear future Johnny, I am very, very sorry." Have you written code that came back to haunt you? If so, click here to send us an email to share your story. We promise to handle it carefully so contributing won't haunt your career. ®
